text: A utility token exists to perform a specific function the protocol needs, independent of any voting rights: gas or fee payment, access to a feature, staking collateral for a role, or a fee discount. None of these require any say in how the protocol changes — its value comes from needing it, not from controlling anything.

A governance token grants voting rights over the protocol itself: proposal rights, voting power weighted by tokens held or delegated, treasury control over accumulated reserves, and parameter changes — adjusting rate curves or emission schedules through a vote instead of a centralized decision.

A governance token's value is speculative on future decisions — it's worth something because holding it lets you influence outcomes that affect the protocol's revenue or survival. In practice, very few tokens are purely one or the other; a single token commonly does double duty as both utility and governance.

Value accrual often works through a fee switch — a governance-controlled mechanism routing a share of protocol revenue to token holders, usually via buyback-and-burn: the protocol uses collected fees to buy its own token on the open market, then burns it.

Say a protocol collects $500,000 in fees this month, and governance has voted to route 20% to the fee switch. That's a $100,000 buyback budget. At a $2.50 token price, that buys and burns 40,000 tokens.

This ties straight back to Lesson 19's deflationary supply models — a fee switch is one of the most common ways a real-revenue burn actually gets implemented, and whether to turn it on is itself a governance decision.
